newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Winkelhaak hopes to reach deep gold ore.
newsitem.headline: Winkelhaak hopes to reach deep gold ore.

text.p: Winkelhaak Mines Ltd hopes to give the ageing mine a second wind by reaching a deep ore body which could yield 96 tonnes of gold, Winkelhaak general manager John Bredenhann said on Tuesday.
If the mine gets the go-ahead to proceed with the deepening of the current Number 6 shaft, it could lay open a further 15 million tonnes of ore and extend the mine's life by 15 years.
"By the first quarter of next year a decision will be made (on number 6 shaft)," Bredenhann told mining analysts on a visit to the mine.
The project will extend the life of the mine from the current eight to 15 years.
Bredenhann said reaching the ore body of the Kimberley reef, about 2.5 km below the surface, could be done either by cutting through declines or sinking a shaft from the existing number 6 shaft.
At present the use of the decline method is preferable because of a massive underground water body in the area.
Mine projections show that the cost of the project would be in the region of 560 million rand over a four year period, at least half of which would have to be financed by outside capital.
If the project is approved, it should take 24 months to reach the reef while sinking the vertical shaft would take about 28 months.
"We are talking two-and-a-half-years down the road," Bredenhann said.
Winkelhaak, which recently posted its first profit after consecutive loss-making quarters, planned to lift distributable income considerably in the six months to end-June 1997.

Bredenhann said the mine had forecast distributable income in the December quarter to be in the region of two million rand, rising to eight million rand in the quarter to end-March 1997 and 12 million rand in the quarter to end-June 1997.
The mine also hoped to make inroads into sweeping up the thousands of tonnes of "sweepings" (crushed gold ore left behind in dormant mining areas) and extract gold from it.
Mine officials said projections showed some 970 kg of gold could be contained in the sweepings in mined-out areas of Winkelhaak.
"It (sweeping) is saving a lot of mines, especially the marginal ones," Bredenhann added.
Presently miners collect the crushed ore using water jets and industrial vacuum cleaners, but Bredenhann said Winkelhaak planned to use outside contractors in future.
Winkelhaak, managed by Gencor Ltd, was first mined in 1955 and is the oldest gold mine on the Evander gold fields.
